title: The Enduring Impact of the American Dust Bowl: Short- and Long-Run Adjustments to Environmental Catastrophe
research_question: What were the short-run and long-run economic consequences of severe soil erosion on agricultural land values, agricultural revenues, and land-use decisions in affected areas? To what extent did affected economies adjust through reallocation of agricultural production versus through migration and shifts to non-agricultural sectors, and what factors limited or facilitated such adjustments?
data_description: The analysis uses a balanced panel of 769 counties across 12 Plains states (Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, Montana, Nebraska, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Texas, Wyoming) observed from 1910 through the 1990s, using 1910 county borders held fixed over time. County-level agricultural, population, and industrial variables come from the U.S. Census of Agriculture and Population (Gutmann 2005; Haines 2005), including per-acre farmland values, agricultural revenues, cropland and pasture acreage, crop-specific output and acreage (wheat, hay, corn, cotton), livestock counts, capital/equipment values, farm sizes, fallow land, tenancy, population, rural and farm population, retail sales, manufacturing employment, payroll, establishments, value added, and unemployment. Additional sources include FDIC banking data (1920–1936), New Deal expenditure data from the Office of Government Reports, and Palmer Drought Severity Index and temperature data from the National Climatic Data Center. Erosion classifications (low, medium, high) come from a Soil Conservation Service map digitized via GIS.
institutional_context: During the 1930s, the American Plains experienced an unprecedented environmental catastrophe known as the Dust Bowl, in which the combination of severe drought (particularly in 1934 and 1936) and decades of intensive cultivation of native grasslands led to massive wind and water erosion of topsoil. By the 1940s, many Plains areas had cumulatively lost more than 75% of their original topsoil, with damage varying substantially across counties even within the same state. The catastrophe overlapped with the Great Depression, restricting credit availability as more-eroded counties experienced more bank failures. Federal responses evolved from the 1933 Agricultural Adjustment Act's price-support and acreage-reduction programs to soil-conservation-oriented policies under the 1935–36 Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Acts and the 1938 AAA, administered through the newly created Soil Conservation Service, which promoted converting cropland to grassland, strip cropping, fallowing, terracing, and windbreaks.
